newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thousands mourn HK protester dead off Japan isles.
newsitem.headline: Thousands mourn HK protester dead off Japan isles.

text.p: Tens of thousands of people holding candles, many sobbing with grief, streamed into a Hong Kong park on Sunday night to mourn a protest leader who drowned last week in a dispute over a group of East China Sea islands.

Activist David Chan was killed last Thursday when he jumped off a protest ship in defiance of a Japanese blockade near the uninhabited rocky outcrops which Japan calls the Senkakus and which China claims as the Diaoyu isles.

For the third time in two weeks, crowds poured out their anger and dramatised a cause that united rival pro-China, pro-Taiwan and pro-democracy camps in the British-ruled territory, which is populated mainly by Chinese.
Mourning banners were strung across the soccer pitches of Hong Kong's Victoria Park and several Chinese communist red flags with golden stars bobbed among the tearful crowd.

Japan has claimed the islands northeast of Taiwan since 1895 and China has claimed them for centuries. Both governments, reluctant to wreck their relations over the issue, are at a loss how to deal with the two-month-old wave of nationalist passion that has swept Chinese communities in East Asia.
The 45-year-old media consultant's body was flown home to a hero's welcome on Friday. A new protest flotilla carrying 50 activists will set sail in a week's time.
"He lived a great life and died a hero," said 70-year-old Lily Sum as she joined the outpouring of grief by a crowd that government radio put at 20,000 and organisers at 40,0000 strong.
"My heart is sorrowful, when I see his face tears well up in my eyes," she said.

A big photo of Chan, dozens of wreaths and a wooden trunk symbolising his coffin, decked in a communist Chinese red flag, stood under a banner in Chinese characters with the words, "Profound condolences on David Chan's death". Other banners carried the slogan "Eternal glory to David Chan".

Chan's wife Lau shun-hing, his eight-year-old son and 10-year-old daughter, as well as his six brothers and sisters, were mobbed by people offering condolences. The widow, a black shawl draped over shoulders, convulsed and sobbed in grief.
"Whatever the public say about his death, it has woken all Chinese around the world to this issue," his brother Tony said.

"Chan is the first casualty. There is no doubt he was a pioneer in the "Protection of the Diaoyu Islands' movement," Chan's co-campaigner Andy Tse said, addressing the crowd, as the weeping widow listened and held her daughter's hand.

The crowd, including politicians from across the spectrum and representatives of China's de facto embassy in Hong Kong, stood with their candles for three minutes of silence and gave three traditional bows in respect of the dead protest leader.
The crowd watched a film of Chan's life and fatal voyage. "I want my children to grow up and become like their father -- a courageous Chinese," Chan's wife said, breaking down.
Patriotic Chinese songs rang out, "Arise Chinese sons and daughters, We are angry now, We'll protect the Diaoyu Islands".

Hundreds of police were deployed with thousands more on standby in case anti-Japanese emotions turned nasty. Japan's consulate on Thursday asked for special protection for Japanese properties and businesses in Hong Kong, fearing a backlash.
Pro-China politician Tsang Yok-shing broke down in tears in mid-speech, saying: "We must fight Japanese militarism...Martyr Chan has given his life for China and the Chinese people."
Loud applause rang out from the crowd as speaker after speaker called on Chinese everywhere to unite for the crusade.
